analysis.one_liner: Bars death sentences imposed or carried out in racially disproportionate patterns, provable by statistics alone.
analysis.headline: The Racial Justice Act never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee in the 101st Congress despite 20 sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred federal, state, and local governments from imposing or carrying out the death penalty in a racially disproportionate pattern — for example, executing one race's members more often than others' convicted of the same crimes, or seeking death more often when victims were of one race. Defendants could prove the pattern with ordinary statistics, without showing that any official intended to discriminate, and the government would then have to explain the disparity with clear evidence of non-racial causes. The bill also required every government with a death penalty to collect race data on all death-eligible cases, guaranteed lawyers and expert help for poor prisoners raising these claims in federal court, and let prisoners raise the claims even if they had not raised them before.
analysis.who_benefits: People facing death sentences — who are overwhelmingly poor, since the bill's own subject list includes the poor and the right to counsel — and especially Black defendants and victims' communities, because the pattern the bill targets is death being sought and carried out more often based on the race of the defendant or the victim. It also benefits families of minority victims whose killers were statistically less likely to face a death sentence. All of them gain a federal remedy where none existed: statistics alone could establish the claim, and a lawyer would be appointed for anyone who could not afford one.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any government from imposing or carrying out a death sentence in a racially disproportionate pattern — either more often against people of one race convicted of the same crimes, or more often for crimes against victims of one race.

Lets a defendant prove the pattern with ordinary statistical evidence and without showing that any individual or institution acted with discriminatory intent; once the defendant makes that showing, the government must explain the disparity with clear and convincing evidence of non-racial factors or the death sentence cannot stand.

Requires every government with a death penalty to designate a central agency to collect standardized data on every death-eligible case — including the race of defendants and victims and every charging, plea, and sentencing decision — and to make the compiled data publicly available in machine-readable form.

Guarantees court-appointed lawyers and publicly funded investigative and expert services for any indigent person raising a claim under the Act in federal habeas court — protection that matters because capital defendants are largely people who could not afford counsel of their own.

Removes the normal rule that state court factual findings are presumed correct in federal court unless the state has kept the required death-penalty data and gave the defendant counsel and investigative help equivalent to the federal standard, so states that do not comply lose deference.
Lets prisoners raise these claims even if they never raised them before enactment, so people already on death row when the bill passed could still use it.

analysis.who_pays: Governments and their prosecutors. Prosecutors would lose the ability to seek or carry out death sentences wherever statistics show a racial skew they cannot explain, and every local official handling a death-eligible case would have to complete a standard data form and turn over police and investigative reports within three months. Governments would also fund appointed counsel and expert services in federal court for poor prisoners raising these claims. State courts would face federal scrutiny of their findings if their state failed to comply.

drawbacks.text: Because the bill expressly does not require proof that anyone acted with discriminatory intent, a defendant could void a death sentence using statistics alone, even if nothing improper happened in his own case — a deliberate trade-off critics of statistical tests have long argued goes too far.

The compliance burden is heavy: every local official responsible for investigating or prosecuting a death-eligible case must file a standard form and a copy of all police and investigative reports within three months of any disposition, and central agencies must compile, index, and publish the data, which is a real administrative cost for state and local governments.

The bill is retroactive — it says prior failure to raise the claim is no bar — so long-final cases could be reopened years after conviction, straining courts and victims' families' expectations of finality.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was potentially life and death: a federal check on executions carried out in racially skewed patterns, in a system where — as the bill's structure acknowledges — defendants are mostly poor and could not otherwise prove discrimination without statistical evidence. The costs are real but bounded: administrative data collection, funded defense services, and a harder path for prosecutors who want to keep death sentences that statistics cannot explain. The bill was not a repeal of capital punishment; it built in a government rebuttal (clear and convincing non-racial explanations) and tied federal deference to state compliance, which gives states a path to keep their systems. Coming two years after the Supreme Court held in McCleskey v. Kemp (1987) that statistical evidence of racial disparity was not enough to overturn a death sentence absent proof of intent, this bill would have legislatively reversed that rule. It never got far enough for those trade-offs to be tested in a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. introduced the Racial Justice Act on May 24, 1989, with 11 original cosponsors including Nancy Pelosi and Leon Panetta.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day; that referral is the last action ever recorded on it.
It attracted 19 cosponsors — 18 Democrats and 1 Republican — but the Judiciary Committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prosecutors and governments kept the death-penalty system exactly as it was, with no data requirements, no statistical challenge process, and no federally funded counsel for prisoners claiming racial bias — so anyone who might have been spared execution under the bill's standard remained exposed to it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, so sponsorship is the only partisan signal: 19 of the bill's 20 sponsors were Democrats, with just one Republican cosponsor among 175 House Republicans.

Their interest in the unexamined status quo ran directly against the defendants and victims' communities the bill would have protected.

industries.note: They would bear the cost of standing up data systems and standard forms for every death-eligible case, but the bill also rewarded compliance: a state that kept the data and provided counsel kept the presumption that its court findings are correct.

Courts would have to appoint counsel and furnish publicly funded investigative and expert services for every indigent prisoner raising a claim under the Act, a new stream of work and resources for defense lawyers and investigators.
